transcript:
[00:00] Aisha: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Aisha from Redwood, and with me is Liam our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Michael: Good, thanks. Michael here from Atlas. We are keen to see how batching and KV caching can drop our token costs without killing p95 latency.
[00:14] Priya: yep, Priya. We have a couple of endpoints, one short chat completion for support (90% of calls) and a long context summarizer for compliance (10%). QPS is around 45 at peak, bursts to 120 for support.
[00:28] Liam: great, that's helpful. quick outline: we'll walk through Redwood Optimize recommendations—batching profiles, prefix/KV cache, cost model spreadsheet—then Q&A and next steps.
[00:40] Michael: sounds good.
[01:05] Liam: first, batching. The basic idea is to group requests into micro-batches to improve GPU utilization. For chat-like short responses we default to micro-batches of 8-16 with a 20-40ms batching window which keeps p95 ~ under 220ms on our 8xA100 sku, but reduces token cost by roughly 25-35% depending on token lengths.
[01:32] Priya: does that assume we can tolerate extra latency from the batching window? our SLA is 200ms p95 for support.
[01:41] Liam: yes, so for 200ms p95 we recommend an adaptive policy: target micro-batch 8 but with latency floor of 150ms; if queue wait exceeds 30ms we flush early. That's where Redwood's adaptive batching helps—it trades throughput for latency when needed.
[02:05] Michael: ok. and for the long summarizer?
[02:11] Liam: long context workloads benefit more from KV/prefix cache. We saw customers get 40-60% token savings by caching repeated prefixes and reuse of KV cache across similar sessions. For compliance summarizer, if the prefix (policy text) is constant across requests, we can avoid re-encoding that segment.
[02:32] Priya: can you explain the difference between prefix cache and KV cache again? sometimes folks confuse them.
[02:38] Liam: sure. prefix cache is basically caching the embedding/encoder outputs for a fixed prompt segment; KV cache caches the attention key/value tensors to skip recomputation between tokens for the same sequence, which is most valuable for long, repeated contexts. In practice we use both: prefix caching for repeated static segments and KV cache to accelerate autoregressive decoding when sessions reuse initial segments.
[03:05] Michael: whats the memory overhead on the server for KV cache? will it push us to bigger instance classes?
[03:12] Liam: yes, KV cache increases memory proportional to sequence length and batch size. For our models, roughly 3-5GB per 2048 tokens per batch per replica depending on quant and model. So if you increase batch from 8->16 you multiply KV footprint. That's why Optimize recommends quant profiles and model variant selection with a memory-aware batching cap.
[03:37] Priya: got it. and during bursts what's the best fallback? we don't want to miss SLAs.
[03:43] Aisha: common pattern: primary route to dedicated pool with aggressive batching and caching; fallback route to hosted low-latency pool without batching (higher cost). Redwood routing policies can failover by latency or capacity to keep SLOs.
[04:03] Michael: ok that helps. show me the cost model... 
[04:10] Liam: we shared a spreadsheet; key columns are tokens_in, tokens_out, qps, batching_factor, cache_hit_rate, model_unit_cost, and estimated monthly cost. For example, at qps 45, batching factor 12, cache hit 30% we estimated 28% lower monthly spend vs no-batching/no-cache.
[04:35] Priya: that's promising. how accurate are these estimates? do you calibrate them to our traffic patterns?
[04:41] Liam: yes, they're templates initially. best practice: run a short benchmark with your sample payloads (we recommend 1-2 hours of replay) on a representative pool and measure real tokens/sec and latency; we then tune batching windows and cache sizes.
[05:00] Michael: about cold cache: if a new session hits cold, is there a big spike in latency for the first few calls?
[05:07] Liam: cold starts can add 50-200ms depending on model and payload. For large prefix caches, first request pays encode cost; subsequent ones benefit. For critical SLO endpoints we recommend a warm-up policy or sticky routing to keep hot replicas.
[05:25] Sara: our infra is strict about memory and we prefer smaller instance classes; can Redwood Optimize give recommended instance sizes vs cost?
[05:33] Aisha: yes, part of the deliverable is a recommended instance matrix: model variant -> batch size cap -> estimated memory -> expected p95. We'll include recommended quantization levels to reduce memory.
[05:47] Priya: about quantization—are certain models unsupported for KV cache with 8-bit quant?
[05:53] Liam: some older kernels had issues, but our runtime supports KV cache with int8/4-bit quant variants for most Llama-family and Mistral-ish models. We'll flag any compatibility issues in the spreadsheet.
[06:10] Michael: how do you measure quality regressions if we change quant or model variant?
[06:16] Liam: Redwood Optimize ties into evals. We recommend a small eval suite: 200 prompts sampled from production with business metrics (classification accuracy, hallucination rate, token overlap). We run regressions when applying quant or switching model. If you want we can help craft the evals.
[06:35] Priya: yes please.
[06:40] Aisha: quick check—what are your major priorities? cost reduction, strict latency, or model accuracy?
[06:47] Michael: priority order: latency SLOs first, then cost, then slight accuracy tweaks acceptable but not regressions.
[06:55] Liam: great—so conservative batching with low latency floor, plus prefix caching where possible is the recommended route.
[07:05] [07:30] (-- short demo share screens --)
[07:45] Liam: walking through the Optimize console: here is the batching profile UI, you can set default batch size, max window ms, and policy: aggressive/adaptive/conservative. The analytics pane shows token-level cost breakdown and effective batch factor over last 24h.
[08:12] Priya: can we set per-route policies? we want different configs for support chat vs summarizer.
[08:18] Liam: yes per-route overrides, you can pin a route to a model variant and batching profile. Also you can tag route as low-latency and it will enforce smaller windows.
[08:35] Michael: about cache eviction—what's strategy for prefix cache if memory is constrained?
[08:40] Liam: LRU by default, but you can pin prefixes as keep-hot for key policy texts. Also TTL-based eviction for rarely used prefixes.
[08:52] Priya: any recommendations on cache size? we have about 1200 distinct templates but most are small.
[08:58] Liam: for 1200 small templates prefix cache memory is light; KV cache is the bigger consumer. We'll recommend a working set size to keep hot templates pinned and estimate bytes per prefix in the spreadsheet.
[09:20] Michael: let's talk numbers—can you run through an example row from the sheet?
[09:25] Liam: sure. baseline: no-batch/no-cache -> tokens/sec 28, monthly cost $12.8k. Optimized: batch=12, cache=30% hit -> tokens/sec 42, monthly cost $9.1k. That assumes model unit cost $0.0003 per token outgoing.
[09:47] Priya: unit cost depends on instance sku and reserved commitment right?
[09:51] Aisha: yes, dedicated reserved capacity lowers unit cost significantly. part of analysis is comparing hosted per-token vs dedicated committed monthly. We'll include both scenarios.
[10:05] Michael: What's the lead time to get a dedicated pool up for benchmarks?
[10:09] Aisha: usually 3-5 business days if we have capacity in region; for new private/on-prem it's longer. For a short benchmark we can spin a hosted dedicated-like pool in your region within 72 hours in most cases.
[10:22] Priya: about data security—can we keep KV cache encrypted at rest? also audit logs?
[10:27] Liam: yes, KV storage and caches are encrypted at rest when using KMS; we also emit audit logs for cache ops in the console and can integrate with your SIEM.
[10:40] Michael: competitor question—some teams tell us Anthropic's infra had better p95 for long context, is that something you've seen?
[10:48] Aisha: in public benchmarks, performance varies model-to-model; Redwood focuses on consistent serving and caching which tightens p95 for repeated patterns. We'll include competitor perf notes but benchmarks are best.
[11:05] Priya: ok timing and orchestration—if we enable caching and increase batch sizes, how do we roll out safely to avoid regressions?
[11:12] Liam: we advise canary rollout: enable caching for 5% traffic, monitor latency and quality evals; if stable, increase to 20%, then 50%, then full. Redwood Console has rollout controls and automatic rollback on metric drift.
[11:29] Michael: that automation helps. Are there observability hooks for tracing token-level latency?
[11:35] Liam: yes, token-level traces, per-route breakouts, and attribution to batching wait vs model compute vs network are available in the Console.
[11:45] Priya: for the summarizer, we do chunked decoding—does KV cache interfere with chunking?
[11:52] Liam: chunked decoding can still use KV cache per chunk, but you need to stitch KV segments carefully. Our runtime supports stitched KV and re-use where possible; we'll include specific config examples.
[12:05] Michael: any gotchas with beam search or sampling when using caching?
[12:11] Liam: caching mainly helps autoregressive decoding; beam search increases memory since you replicate KV per beam. For high beam widths caching gains diminish; Optimize will flag beam costs.
[12:25] Priya: do you have any examples of customers in financial services using prefix caches? worried about PII.
[12:31] Aisha: yes, we have banks using prefix cache for policy texts; key is to tokenize and treat PII as non-cacheable segments. Redwood supports per-prompt redaction policies and cache partitioning by tenant.
[12:50] Michael: about billing—if we cache, do we get billed on tokens_out only or also cached tokens when hits occur?
[12:58] Liam: billing is based on model compute actually executed. On cache hit we avoid re-encoding so you're billed only for the tokens decoded (outgoing) plus marginal overhead; the spreadsheet models that.
[13:10] Priya: ok. let's go through the benchmark plan—what do you need from us?
[13:16] Liam: we need sample payloads (support chats and summarizer examples), target SLO numbers, expected peak qps, and a list of routes to test. Also decide whether you want hosted or dedicated pool for the run.
[13:30] Michael: we'll share payloads and SLOs by Monday.
[13:36] Aisha: perfect. we'll prepare the spreadsheet and a recommended initial batching profile and cache config.
[13:42] [14:00] (slight crosstalk, background noise)
[14:10] Michael: one more question—if we get a 30% cache hit do we need to provision fewer replicas?
[14:17] Liam: cache hits reduce compute but KV still consumes memory; depending on hit rate your throughput per replica increases which can reduce replica count; our cost model will estimate replica counts vs hit rates.
[14:33] Priya: any recommended A/B test design for cost vs latency?
[14:38] Aisha: run parallel routes: current config vs optimized for a % of traffic, collect both latency and business metrics for 48-72 hours, then compare. Optimize provides variance-aware comparisons.
[14:53] Michael: ok. let's recap next steps.
[14:58] Aisha: recap: Redwood sends cost model + configs by 2026-12-18; Atlas shares payloads and SLOs by 2026-12-20; schedule benchmark w/c 2026-12-27; SE to set up canary plan. Any objections?
[15:15] Priya: none.
[15:18] Michael: ok thanks everyone.
[15:20] Aisha: thanks all. we'll follow up in email with links to the sheet and the demo recording.
[15:25] (meeting ends)
